title: PICS-assisted survey reported seven new Small Magellanic Cloud pulsars
summary: A MeerKAT survey of the Small Magellanic Cloud reported seven new radio pulsars. Each pointing produced hundreds of thousands of folded candidates, too many to inspect by eye. The pipeline partially classified them with PICS, a machine-learning system; a minimum PICS score of 10 per cent and a folded S/N of 7 reduced them to the order of a thousand per pointing, which researchers on the paper then classified by eye before follow-up. The paper does not identify each pulsar’s PICS score, so this is an AI-assisted survey-level result rather than a claim that the model independently discovered all seven sources. The paper also reports pulsar–nebula associations; the later timing paper follows this cohort and is not counted again.
ai_technology: Pulsar Image-based Classification System (PICS), a machine-learning classifier for folded pulsar candidates
organization: The University of Manchester; Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy; South African Radio Astronomy Observatory; INAF-Osservatorio Astronomico di Cagliari; University of Cape Town; Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics; Leibniz University Hannover; Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics; Western Sydney University

source_review.scope: Primary arXiv v1 methods, results and author front matter; peer-reviewed author-deposited journal PDF for publication date, author affiliations and survey result. 2026-11-25 update: candidate counts and thresholds from the arXiv v1 methods; the first author confirmed that the candidates were classified by researchers on the paper.

evidence.tested: The survey reports seven new SMC radio pulsars; candidate triage included PICS filtering followed by human review and observational follow-up.
evidence.unknown: The paper does not report per-pulsar PICS scores; it does not establish model-only detection or that PICS was essential for each individual pulsar.
evidence.ai_role: PICS partially classified folded candidates and filtered the candidate set before human visual classification.
